questions.q: What is the change from gas to liquid called?
questions.why: Condensation is a gas turning into a liquid as it cools.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature?
questions.why: Lighter molecules move faster on average, so the gas with the lowest Mr diffuses fastest.

questions.q: A substance melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C. What state is it at 25 °C?
questions.why: 25 °C is above its melting point and below its boiling point.

questions.q: A gas is sealed in a syringe and heated at constant pressure. Why does its volume increase?
o: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing the plunger out
questions.why: Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy. Faster particles collide with the walls harder and more often, so the gas expands until the pressure is back to its original value.

questions.q: A heating curve for a pure solid has a flat section while it melts. Why does the temperature stay constant?
o: The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to increase their kinetic energy
The heater stops working during melting
The particles stop moving while they melt
Energy is being released by the solid
questions.why: During a change of state the energy breaks the attractions between particles, so their average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, does not rise until melting is complete.

long.q: Describe the arrangement and the motion of the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas.
scheme: B1: solid: particles close together in a regular arrangement (lattice)
B1: solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions
B1: liquid: particles close together in an irregular (random) arrangement
B1: liquid: particles move around and slide past each other
B1: gas: particles far apart in a random arrangement
B1: gas: particles move quickly and randomly in all directions

long.q: A long glass tube has cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube, nearer the hydrochloric acid end. Explain these observations. (Mr: NH₃ = 17, HCl = 36.5)
scheme: B1: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, and the white solid forms where the two gases meet
B1: the gas particles spread through the tube by diffusion, because of their random motion
B1: ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17) than hydrogen chloride (36.5)
B1: so ammonia particles move faster and travel further in the same time, and the ring forms nearer the hydrochloric acid end

long.q: Use the kinetic particle theory to explain why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when the gas is heated.
scheme: B1: the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
B1: they collide with the walls of the container more often
B1: and they hit the walls with greater force, so the pressure increases

long.q: A student melts a solid X in a boiling tube, then lets it cool, recording the temperature every minute. The temperature falls steadily, stays at 54 °C for 4 minutes, then falls again. State the freezing point of X, explain why the temperature stays constant, and state what the results suggest about the purity of X.
scheme: B1: freezing point (and melting point) = 54 °C
B1: while X is freezing, forces of attraction form between the particles and energy is released
B1: this energy released balances the energy lost to the surroundings, so the temperature stays constant
B1: X is pure, because it freezes at a single fixed temperature (an impure substance freezes over a range of temperatures)

long.q: Name the change of state when ice turns into water and when water vapour forms droplets on a cold window. Use the kinetic particle theory to explain why water in a puddle evaporates even though it is well below its boiling point, and why it evaporates faster on a warm day.
scheme: B1: ice to water: melting
B1: water vapour to droplets: condensing (condensation)
B1: particles at the surface with the most kinetic energy can overcome the attractive forces and escape into the air
B1: at a higher temperature more particles have enough energy to escape, so evaporation is faster

questions.q: An atom of sodium has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its nucleon (mass) number?
questions.why: Nucleon number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of chlorine (proton number 17)?
questions.why: Shells fill 2, then 8, then the remaining 7.

questions.q: What type of bonding is in sodium chloride?
questions.why: Electrons transfer from sodium to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by electrostatic attraction.

questions.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
o: Each carbon has one delocalised electron that can move
questions.why: Each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one electron free to move between the layers.

questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
o: The forces between molecules are weak
questions.why: Melting overcomes the weak intermolecular forces, not the strong covalent bonds inside molecules.

questions.q: What are isotopes of an element?
o: Atoms with different numbers of protons
Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms with different numbers of electrons
questions.why: Isotopes share atomic number (protons) and chemical behaviour, but differ in nucleon number (mass) due to neutron count.

long.q: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Define the term isotopes, state the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom of ³⁷Cl (proton number 17), and explain why the two isotopes have the same chemical properties.
scheme: B1: isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
B1: 17 protons
B1: 20 neutrons
B1: 17 electrons
B1: they have the same number of electrons in the outer shell (same electronic configuration), so they react in the same way

long.q: A sample of boron contains 20.0% of atoms of ¹⁰B and 80.0% of atoms of ¹¹B. Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.
scheme: M1: multiply each isotope's mass by its percentage: 10 × 20.0 and 11 × 80.0

long.q: Describe, in terms of electrons, how magnesium (electronic configuration 2,8,2) reacts with oxygen (2,6) to form magnesium oxide. Explain why solid magnesium oxide does not conduct electricity but molten magnesium oxide does.
scheme: B1: each magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons to form a Mg²⁺ ion
B1: each oxygen atom gains two electrons to form an O²⁻ ion (both ions now have full outer shells)
B1: the oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice
B1: in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move
B1: when molten, the ions are free to move and carry the charge

long.q: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon. Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why diamond is very hard and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft and slippery and does conduct electricity.
scheme: B1: in diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant (tetrahedral) structure
B1: strong covalent bonds in all directions make diamond very hard
B1: diamond has no free (delocalised) electrons, so it does not conduct
B1: in graphite each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers, and the fourth outer electron of each atom is delocalised, so graphite conducts
B1: the forces between the layers are weak, so the layers slide over each other, making graphite soft and slippery

long.q: Describe the covalent bonding in a molecule of water, H₂O, and state two physical properties of simple molecular substances such as water.
scheme: B1: a covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms
B1: the oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of the two hydrogen atoms (two single covalent bonds)
B1: each atom then has a full outer shell (noble gas configuration): oxygen 8 electrons, hydrogen 2
B1: low melting and boiling points
B1: poor conductors of electricity

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass of CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16)
How many moles are in 36 g of water? (Mr = 18)
questions.why: moles = mass ÷ Mr = 36 ÷ 18 = 2.

questions.q: What volume does 0.5 mol of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure? (molar volume 24 dm³)
25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised. How many moles of NaOH are there?
questions.why: moles = concentration × volume in dm³ = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250.

questions.q: Which is the balanced equation for magnesium burning?
questions.why: Two Mg and two O on each side.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂? (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some ignored the brackets and worked out 'MgOH₂'. 24 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 58.

long.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide made from 25 g of calcium carbonate. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
scheme: M1: Mr(CaCO₃) = 100, so moles = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25
M1: moles of CaO = 0.25 (1 : 1)

long.q: Explain the difference in melting points between sodium chloride (801 °C) and chlorine (−101 °C) in terms of structure and bonding.
scheme: B1: sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice structure with strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
B1: breaking these strong ionic bonds requires a large amount of thermal energy, giving a very high melting point
B1: chlorine consists of small simple molecules (Cl₂) held together by weak intermolecular van der Waals forces
B1: only a small amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces (covalent bonds within molecules remain unbroken)

long.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol dm⁻³ and in g dm⁻³. (Mr NaOH = 40)
scheme: M1: moles of NaOH = 2 × 0.00300 = 0.00600 mol
A1: concentration = 0.00600 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.240 mol dm⁻³

long.q: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 56. Calculate its empirical formula and its molecular formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
scheme: A1: ratio 1 : 2, so empirical formula CH₂
M1: Mr of CH₂ = 14, and 56 ÷ 14 = 4
A1: molecular formula C₄H₈

long.q: Iron is made by the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. In a test run, 800 kg of iron(III) oxide produced 448 kg of iron. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
scheme: M1: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160, so moles = 800 000 ÷ 160 = 5000 mol
M1: moles of Fe = 2 × 5000 = 10 000 mol, so theoretical mass = 10 000 × 56 = 560 000 g = 560 kg
A1: percentage yield = 448 ÷ 560 × 100 = 80.0%

questions.q: In electrolysis, what forms at the cathode when molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed?
questions.why: Positive Pb²⁺ ions go to the negative cathode and gain electrons to form lead.

questions.q: Why must ionic compounds be molten or dissolved to be electrolysed?
o: So the ions are free to move
So electrons can move through them
questions.why: In a solid the ions are fixed; they must be free to move to carry the current.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, what forms at the anode?
questions.why: With concentrated chloride, chloride ions are discharged at the anode as chlorine.

questions.q: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, what is the only product?
questions.why: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water, releasing electrical energy.

questions.q: Which are the inputs to a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): most candidates thought hydrogen and oxygen were outputs. They are the fuels; water and electrical energy come out.

questions.q: What forms at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common error was 2H instead of H₂. Hydrogen is diatomic; sodium is too reactive to be discharged from water.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide using inert electrodes, what forms at the cathode?
questions.why: Positively charged lead ions (Pb²⁺) gain electrons at the negative cathode to form lead metal: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb.

long.q: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the products at each electrode and write the ionic half-equation at the cathode.
scheme: B1: anode (positive): chlorine
B1: cathode (negative): hydrogen
B1: the solution left contains sodium hydroxide

long.q: 2.43 g of magnesium ribbon is reacted completely with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Calculate the mass of magnesium chloride formed and the volume of hydrogen gas evolved at r.t.p. (Ar: Mg = 24.3, Cl = 35.5; molar gas volume = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
scheme: M1: moles of Mg = 2.43 ÷ 24.3 = 0.100 mol
A1: mass of MgCl₂ = 0.100 × 95.3 = 9.53 g
A1: volume of H₂ = 0.100 × 24.0 = 2.40 dm³

long.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode, write the ionic half-equation for each, and explain why the lead(II) bromide must be molten.
scheme: B1: cathode: lead
B1: anode: bromine (red-brown vapour)
B1: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
B1: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
B1: the ions must be free to move to the electrodes; in the solid they are held in fixed positions

long.q: Describe how a steel spoon can be electroplated with silver, give the half-equation for the reaction at the spoon, and give one reason for electroplating objects.
scheme: B1: the spoon is made the cathode (negative electrode)
B1: the anode is a piece of silver
B1: the electrolyte is a solution containing silver ions, e.g. aqueous silver nitrate
B1: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, so silver is deposited on the spoon
B1: reason: to improve appearance or to resist corrosion

long.q: Give the overall equation for the reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, and give one advantage and two disadvantages of using fuel cells instead of petrol engines in cars.
scheme: B1: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
B1: advantage: the only product is water, so no carbon dioxide or other pollutants are released (or: more efficient)
B1: disadvantage: hydrogen is a flammable gas that is difficult to store, needing high pressure
B1: a second disadvantage, e.g. hydrogen is often made from fossil fuels, there are few refuelling stations, or fuel cells are expensive

questions.q: In an exothermic reaction, the temperature of the surroundings…
questions.why: Exothermic reactions transfer thermal energy to the surroundings.

questions.q: Bond breaking is…
questions.why: Energy must be taken in to break bonds; making bonds releases energy.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = −90 kJ/mol. It is…
questions.why: A negative ΔH means energy is released to the surroundings.

questions.q: Use the bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ/mol to find ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
questions.why: Energy in to break bonds = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; energy out making 2 H–Cl bonds = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: On a reaction pathway diagram, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. Which description is correct?
questions.why: Products with more energy than the reactants means energy was taken in from the surroundings, so the reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive.

long.q: Define the terms exothermic reaction and endothermic reaction, and give one example of each.
scheme: B1: exothermic: a reaction that transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases
B1: example of exothermic, e.g. combustion of a fuel or neutralisation
B1: endothermic: a reaction that takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases
B1: example of endothermic, e.g. thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate or photosynthesis

long.q: Methane burns: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Use these bond energies in kJ mol⁻¹ to calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464.
scheme: M1: energy to break bonds = (4 × 413) + (2 × 498) = 2648 kJ
M1: energy released making bonds = (2 × 805) + (4 × 464) = 3466 kJ

long.q: Describe the reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, stating how the activation energy and the enthalpy change are shown on it.
scheme: B1: the products are at a lower energy than the reactants
B1: the curve rises from the reactants to a peak, then falls to the products
B1: activation energy is the energy difference from the reactants up to the top of the peak
B1: enthalpy change ΔH is the difference between reactants and products, shown by a downward arrow (negative ΔH)

long.q: Describe how a student could measure the temperature change when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and explain why a polystyrene cup is used.
scheme: B1: measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25.0 cm³) of the acid into a polystyrene cup using a measuring cylinder or pipette
B1: record the starting temperature with a thermometer
B1: add a fixed volume of the alkali, stir, and record the highest temperature reached
B1: temperature change = highest temperature − starting temperature
B1: polystyrene (with a lid) is an insulator, so it reduces thermal energy loss to the surroundings

long.q: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why some reactions are exothermic and others are endothermic.
scheme: B1: bond breaking is endothermic: energy is absorbed
B1: bond making is exothermic: energy is released
B1: a reaction is exothermic overall if more energy is released making the bonds in the products than is absorbed breaking the bonds in the reactants (endothermic if the reverse)

questions.q: Which change increases the rate of a reaction between marble chips and acid?
questions.why: Powder has a larger surface area, giving more frequent collisions.

questions.q: What does a catalyst do?
o: It is used up in the reaction
It increases the rate without being used up
questions.why: A catalyst provides a route with lower activation energy and is unchanged at the end.

questions.q: In the Haber process, what is made?
questions.why: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, using an iron catalyst.

questions.q: Oxidation is…
questions.why: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain.

questions.q: For an equilibrium, increasing the pressure shifts the position towards…
o: the side with more moles of gas
the side with fewer moles of gas
questions.why: The equilibrium shifts to reduce the pressure, towards fewer gas molecules.

questions.q: In the Contact process, which conditions are used?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many confused the Contact process with the Haber process (iron catalyst, 20 000 kPa).

long.q: Use collision theory to explain why increasing the concentration of an acid increases the rate of its reaction with magnesium.
scheme: B1: more acid particles in the same volume
B1: so more frequent collisions between particles
B1: more successful collisions per second

long.q: In the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); the forward reaction is exothermic. State the conditions used, and explain the effect of high pressure on the yield of ammonia and why a lower temperature is not used.
scheme: B1: conditions: about 450 °C, 20 000 kPa (200 atm) and an iron catalyst
B1: high pressure moves the position of equilibrium to the right, because there are fewer moles of gas on the right (2 compared with 4), so the yield increases
B1: high pressure also increases the rate of reaction
B1: a lower temperature would give a higher yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic, but the rate would be too slow
B1: 450 °C is a compromise between a good rate and an acceptable yield

long.q: A student adds marble chips to excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask on a balance and records the mass every 30 s. In the first 60 s the mass falls by 0.48 g. Explain why the mass falls, calculate the mean rate in the first 60 s, and predict and explain how the results would change if the same mass of powdered marble were used.
scheme: B1: the mass falls because carbon dioxide gas is produced and escapes from the flask
M1: mean rate = 0.48 ÷ 60
B1: with powder the mass falls faster at the start (steeper curve)
B1: because powder has a larger surface area, so collisions between acid particles and marble are more frequent
B1: the total mass lost is the same, because the same mass of marble reacts (the acid is in excess)

long.q: For the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in terms of oxygen, and state the change in oxidation number of iron. In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, identify the oxidising agent and explain your answer in terms of electrons.
scheme: B1: iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen
B1: carbon monoxide is oxidised because it gains oxygen
B1: the oxidation number of iron falls from +3 to 0
B1: Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent
B1: because it gains electrons from zinc (is reduced), and so oxidises the zinc

long.q: State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change, and describe what a catalyst is, giving one example.
scheme: B1: a chemical change produces a new substance; a physical change does not
B1: a physical change is usually easy to reverse (e.g. melting); many chemical changes are not, and they often involve an energy change
B1: a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end of the reaction
B1: example, e.g. manganese(IV) oxide for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, or iron in the Haber process

questions.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution at 25 °C?
questions.why: pH 7 is neutral; below is acidic, above is alkaline.

questions.q: Which ion is present in all acidic solutions?
questions.why: Acids release hydrogen ions in water.

questions.q: Acid + metal carbonate gives a salt, water and…
questions.why: Carbonates fizz with acids, releasing carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which salt is insoluble in water?
questions.why: Most sulfates dissolve, but barium, calcium and lead sulfates don't.

questions.q: How is an insoluble salt made?
questions.why: Mixing two soluble salts that swap ions forms the insoluble salt as a precipitate.

questions.q: A salt is made by adding excess copper(II) carbonate to dilute sulfuric acid. What is the next step?
o: Filter to remove the excess copper(II) carbonate
Add more acid until it fizzes again
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many crystallised before removing the excess solid. Filter first, then heat the filtrate to the crystallising point.

questions.q: Which salt can be prepared by a precipitation reaction between two aqueous solutions?
questions.why: Insoluble salts like BaSO₄ are prepared by mixing two soluble solutions (e.g. BaCl₂ and Na₂SO₄) to form a solid precipitate.

long.q: Describe how to prepare pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
scheme: B1: warm the acid and add copper(II) oxide until some is left over (excess)
B1: filter to remove the excess copper(II) oxide
B1: heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, to the point of crystallisation
B1: leave to cool so crystals form
B1: filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers

long.q: Use collision theory to explain how increasing the temperature of a reaction mixture increases the rate of reaction.
scheme: B1: particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
B1: collision frequency increases (more collisions per unit time)
B1: significantly more colliding particles possess energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (E ≥ Ea)
B1: a much higher proportion of collisions are successful, which produces a large increase in the reaction rate

long.q: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration are compared. Explain why hydrochloric acid has a lower pH and reacts faster with magnesium ribbon.
scheme: B1: hydrochloric acid is a strong acid: it is completely dissociated in water
B1: ethanoic acid is a weak acid: it is only partially dissociated
B1: so hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions, giving a lower pH
B1: more H⁺ ions mean more frequent collisions with magnesium, so the reaction is faster

long.q: Describe how a student could prepare pure, dry crystals of sodium chloride from dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous sodium hydroxide.
scheme: B1: use a pipette to put 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask and add a few drops of an indicator (e.g. methyl orange)
B1: add acid from a burette until the indicator just changes colour, and record the volume of acid added
B1: repeat with the same volumes of acid and alkali but without the indicator
B1: heat the solution to evaporate some of the water, then leave it to cool and crystallise
B1: filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers

long.q: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry sample of the insoluble salt barium sulfate, and write the ionic equation for the reaction.
scheme: B1: mix aqueous solutions of a soluble barium salt (e.g. barium chloride) and a soluble sulfate (e.g. sodium sulfate)
B1: filter the mixture to collect the precipitate
B1: wash the precipitate with distilled water and dry it (in a warm oven or between filter papers)
B1: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

questions.q: Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group because…
o: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily
they have more protons attracting the electron
questions.why: Shielding and distance make the single outer electron easier to lose.

questions.q: Which halogen is a dark grey solid at room temperature?
questions.why: Iodine is a grey-black solid; chlorine is a gas and bromine a red-brown liquid.

questions.q: Chlorine is bubbled into potassium bromide solution. What happens?
o: Bromine is displaced and the solution turns orange
questions.why: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salts.

questions.q: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
o: They have full outer shells of electrons
questions.why: A full outer shell is stable, so they don't need to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.q: Elements in the same group have the same number of…
questions.why: The group number (for groups 1 to 7) is the number of outer electrons.

questions.q: What is the state of bromine at room temperature and pressure?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common misconception is that bromine is a gas. It is a red-brown liquid that gives off a vapour.

long.q: Explain why the Group I metals become more reactive down the group.
scheme: B1: the atoms get larger, with more electron shells
B1: so the outer electron is further from the nucleus / more shielded, less strongly attracted
B1: so it is lost more easily

long.q: Chlorine water is added to colourless aqueous potassium bromide. Describe what is seen, write the ionic equation, and explain the reaction. State and explain what happens if aqueous iodine is added to potassium bromide instead.
scheme: B1: the solution turns from colourless to orange (yellow-orange)
B1: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
B1: chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from its compound
B1: with iodine there is no reaction, because iodine is less reactive than bromine

long.q: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive, and give one use each of argon and helium.
scheme: B1: they have a full outer shell of electrons (a stable electronic configuration), so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons
B1: argon: filling lamps (or giving an inert atmosphere, e.g. for welding)
B1: helium: filling balloons or airships (low density and not flammable)

long.q: State four properties of the transition elements that are different from those of the Group I metals.
scheme: B1: higher densities
B1: higher melting points
B1: they form coloured compounds
B1: they (and their compounds) often act as catalysts

long.q: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. Use this to deduce its group and period in the Periodic Table, identify the element, and state whether it is a metal or a non-metal, with a reason.
scheme: B1: Group VI, because it has 6 electrons in its outer shell
B1: Period 3, because it has 3 occupied electron shells
B1: the element is sulfur
B1: non-metal, because it is on the right of the Periodic Table (it gains electrons to form negative ions / forms an acidic oxide)

questions.q: Which metal is extracted from its ore by electrolysis, not by carbon?
questions.why: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide.

questions.q: Why are alloys often harder than pure metals?
o: Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers so they can't slide easily
questions.why: Atoms of a different size stop the layers sliding over one another.

questions.q: What two things are needed for iron to rust?
questions.why: Rusting needs both oxygen (air) and water.

questions.q: Galvanising protects iron by coating it with…
questions.why: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes in place of the iron (sacrificial protection).

questions.q: Which metal does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not recall that copper does not react with dilute acids; it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

long.q: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium, referring to their electronic configurations.
scheme: B1: sodium has electron configuration 2,8,1; potassium has 2,8,8,1
B1: potassium's outer valence electron is in a higher principal energy level (fourth shell vs third shell)
B1: potassium's outer electron is further from the positive nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells
B1: the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker, so potassium loses its outer electron more readily

long.q: Describe the extraction of iron from hematite in the blast furnace, including equations for the main reactions.
scheme: B1: raw materials: hematite (Fe₂O₃), coke (C), limestone (CaCO₃) and hot air
B1: coke burns in the hot air, releasing heat: C + O₂ → CO₂
B1: carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide: CO₂ + C → 2CO
B1: carbon monoxide reduces the iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
B1: limestone decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
B1: calcium oxide removes sandy impurities as slag: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃

long.q: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon. Describe the role of cryolite, write the half-equations at each electrode, and explain why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly.
scheme: B1: aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
B1: aluminium oxide (from purified bauxite) is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers the operating temperature and saves energy
B1: cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
B1: anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
B1: the oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away

long.q: A student sets up three test tubes, each with an iron nail. Tube A: nail in tap water, open to the air. Tube B: nail in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. Tube C: nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride, stoppered. Predict in which tube(s) the nail rusts and explain the results.
scheme: B1: only the nail in tube A rusts
B1: in tube B, boiling removed dissolved air (oxygen) from the water and the oil stops air dissolving again, so no rust
B1: in tube C, the calcium chloride absorbs water vapour, so the air is dry and there is no rust
B1: the stopper stops moist air getting into tube C
B1: conclusion: both water and oxygen are needed for iron to rust

long.q: Describe metallic bonding and use it to explain why metals conduct electricity and are malleable. Explain why an alloy such as brass is harder than the pure metals it is made from.
scheme: B1: metallic bonding: a lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons
B1: held together by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons
B1: metals conduct because the delocalised electrons move through the structure and carry the charge
B1: metals are malleable because layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bonding
B1: in an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide as easily, making it harder

questions.q: Which gas from car engines causes acid rain?
questions.why: Nitrogen oxides (and sulfur dioxide) dissolve in rain to form acids.

questions.q: What is the main gas in clean dry air?
questions.why: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

questions.q: Which two gases are greenhouse gases?
questions.why: Carbon dioxide and methane absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.

questions.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
questions.why: Chlorine kills bacteria in water treatment.

questions.q: How does methane add to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
o: It reflects sunlight back to space
It absorbs thermal energy emitted by the Earth and re-emits some back towards the Earth
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers often confused the greenhouse effect with ozone or acid rain.

questions.q: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?
questions.why: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single C–C bonds, sharing the general formula C_n H_{2n+2}.

long.q: Describe two chemical tests for the presence of water, and describe how you could show that a sample of water is pure.
scheme: B1: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue
B1: anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride turns from blue to pink
B1: pure water boils at exactly 100 °C
B1: pure water melts (freezes) at exactly 0 °C

long.q: Describe the stages in the treatment of water from a river to make it suitable for drinking, and state the purpose of each.
scheme: B1: sedimentation and filtration (through gravel and sand) remove solids
B1: carbon (activated carbon) removes tastes and odours
B1: chlorination (adding chlorine) kills microbes
B1: the water is then stored and piped to homes, now safe to drink (or: pH may be adjusted)

long.q: Explain how increasing amounts of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere lead to climate change. Name a source of each gas and give two strategies to reduce the effects.
scheme: B1: carbon dioxide comes from the combustion of fossil fuels; methane from cattle, rice fields or decomposition of vegetation/landfill
B1: these gases absorb thermal (infrared) energy radiated from the Earth's surface
B1: they re-emit it, so less thermal energy escapes to space and the average temperature rises (enhanced greenhouse effect)
B1: this leads to climate change, e.g. melting ice, rising sea levels or more extreme weather
B1: two strategies, e.g. using renewable energy instead of fossil fuels, planting trees, reducing livestock farming

long.q: Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in car engines, state one harmful effect, and describe how a catalytic converter removes them.
scheme: B1: at the high temperature in the engine, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
B1: harmful effect, e.g. acid rain, photochemical smog or respiratory problems
B1: in the catalytic converter, nitrogen monoxide reacts with carbon monoxide
B1: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂
B1: the catalyst, e.g. platinum or rhodium, speeds up the reaction so harmless nitrogen is released

long.q: Explain why farmers use NPK fertilisers. Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, and in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, and state which supplies more nitrogen per kilogram. (Ar: N = 14, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
scheme: B1: NPK fertilisers supply the elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, replacing those removed by crops, for improved plant growth and higher yields
B1: ammonium nitrate supplies more nitrogen per kilogram

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.why: Alkanes are saturated: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, e.g. methane CH₄.

questions.q: Which test shows a compound is unsaturated?
o: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless
questions.why: Alkenes add across the C=C double bond, decolourising bromine water.

questions.q: What is the main use of fractional distillation of petroleum?
o: To separate it into fractions with different boiling ranges
questions.why: Fractions condense at different heights of the column according to boiling range.

questions.q: Ethanol can be made by fermentation of…
questions.why: Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide, around 25–35 °C, without oxygen.

questions.q: What type of polymerisation makes poly(ethene)?
questions.why: Ethene molecules add together by opening their double bonds; nothing else is formed.

questions.q: What type of reaction happens when ethene reacts with bromine?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not recall this. Bromine adds across the C=C bond, which is why the orange colour disappears.

long.q: Ethene can be made into poly(ethene). Name this type of polymerisation and describe a test that shows ethene is unsaturated.
scheme: B1: addition polymerisation
B1: add bromine water
B1: it changes from orange to colourless

long.q: Describe the conditions used for cracking, explain why it is carried out, and write an equation for cracking decane, C₁₀H₂₂, to form octane and ethene.
scheme: B1: high temperature with a catalyst
B1: large alkane molecules are broken down into smaller alkanes and alkenes
B1: because demand for smaller molecules (e.g. petrol) is greater than supply, and alkenes are needed to make polymers
B1: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄

long.q: Describe how petroleum is separated into fractions, and name two fractions with a use for each.
scheme: B1: petroleum is heated so it vaporises and enters a fractionating column
B1: the column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top
B1: fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points (smaller molecules higher up)
B1: one fraction and its use, e.g. refinery gas for heating and cooking, gasoline for car fuel, naphtha as a chemical feedstock
B1: a second fraction and its use, e.g. kerosene for jet fuel, diesel oil for diesel engines, fuel oil for ships, bitumen for road surfaces

long.q: Ethanol can be made by fermentation of glucose or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene. Give an equation and conditions for each method, and compare the two methods.
scheme: B1: fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, using yeast at 25–35 °C without air
B1: hydration: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, using steam at about 300 °C, 6000 kPa and a phosphoric acid catalyst
B1: fermentation uses renewable raw materials (sugar from plants)
B1: fermentation is slow, a batch process, and gives a dilute solution that must be distilled
B1: hydration is fast, continuous and gives pure ethanol, but uses ethene from petroleum, a non-renewable resource

long.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol when warmed with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. Name the type of compound formed and the product, state the role of the sulfuric acid, and write the equation.
scheme: B1: an ester
B1: ethyl ethanoate
B1: the concentrated sulfuric acid is a catalyst
B1: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

questions.q: In chromatography, how is the Rf value worked out?
o: distance moved by solvent ÷ distance moved by spot
distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent
questions.why: Rf = distance travelled by the substance ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front.

questions.q: How would you separate salt from salt solution?
questions.why: Evaporating the water leaves the salt crystals behind.

questions.q: Which gas turns limewater milky?
questions.why: CO₂ forms insoluble calcium carbonate with limewater.

questions.q: A flame test gives a lilac flame. Which ion is present?
questions.why: Potassium gives lilac; sodium yellow, lithium red, calcium orange-red.

questions.q: Adding aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a light blue precipitate. Which ion?
questions.why: Copper(II) hydroxide is light blue; iron(II) is green and iron(III) red-brown.

questions.q: Which test identifies chlorine gas?
o: Add acidified silver nitrate: white precipitate
A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
Damp blue litmus paper turns red then is bleached
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the test for chlorine gas was often confused with the test for chloride ions (silver nitrate).

long.q: Describe how paper chromatography can be used to find out whether a food colouring is a mixture of dyes. In the chromatogram one spot moved 4.2 cm and the solvent front moved 6.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value of this spot.
scheme: B1: draw a baseline in pencil (ink would dissolve and run)
B1: put a small spot of the food colouring on the baseline
B1: stand the paper in solvent with the solvent level below the baseline, so the spot does not dissolve into the solvent
B1: remove the paper when the solvent is near the top and mark the solvent front; more than one spot shows a mixture
M1: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 4.2 ÷ 6.0

long.q: Rock salt is a mixture of sodium chloride and sand. Describe how to obtain dry crystals of sodium chloride from rock salt.
scheme: B1: crush the rock salt, add water and stir (warm) so the sodium chloride dissolves
B1: filter to remove the sand, which stays on the filter paper as the residue
B1: heat the filtrate to evaporate some of the water, until crystals start to form
B1: leave to cool and crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals between filter papers

long.q: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to solution X and a red-brown precipitate forms. Dilute nitric acid and aqueous barium nitrate are added to a second sample of X and a white precipitate forms. Identify X, write the ionic equation for the formation of the red-brown precipitate, and explain why the nitric acid is added.
scheme: B1: red-brown precipitate shows iron(III) ions, Fe³⁺
B1: white precipitate with acidified barium nitrate shows sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻
B1: X is iron(III) sulfate
B1: Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
B1: the acid removes carbonate ions, which would also give a white precipitate with barium ions

long.q: Describe the tests, with positive results, for hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, ammonia and chlorine.
scheme: B1: hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
B1: oxygen: relights a glowing splint
B1: carbon dioxide: turns limewater milky (cloudy white)
B1: ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue
B1: chlorine: bleaches damp litmus paper

long.q: Describe how to carry out a titration to find the volume of dilute hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide accurately. A student's titres were 23.0 cm³ (rough), 22.10 cm³, 22.20 cm³ and 22.15 cm³. Calculate the mean titre to use.
scheme: B1: use a pipette to transfer 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask
B1: add a few drops of a suitable indicator, e.g. methyl orange or thymolphthalein
B1: add the acid from a burette while swirling, drop by drop near the end-point, until the indicator just changes colour
B1: read the burette at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, and repeat until concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³) are obtained
M1: ignore the rough titre and average the concordant titres: (22.10 + 22.20 + 22.15) ÷ 3
